Q: npm check and update package if needed A:

One easy step:

npm i -g npm-check-updates && ncu -u && npm i

That is all. All of the package versions in file package.json will be the latest major versions.

What is happening here?

  1. Installing a package that checks updates for you.

  2. Use this package to update all package versions in your package.json file (-u is short for --updateAll).

  3. Install all of the new versions of the packages.

Q: How to write the \U unicode format in Python regex A:

This is rather unrelated to regex but only to the way of using \u and \U prefixes in Python strings.

In plain text, the Unicode characters are commonly represented as U + code, for example U+0041 for the character A. But inside Python strings, you can use either \u followed with 4 hexadecimal digits or \U followed with 8 ones. For example you can write '\u0041\U00000042' to get 'AB'. Or simply \x followed with 2 hexa digits if the code point is less than 256: '\x41', still for 'A'.

Q: Latency of assembly memory ops in modern CPUs A:

The c9x.me pages are mostly scraped from some old version1 of Intel's vol.2 PDF, but the latency/throughput numbers are added by someone, for very old CPUs, I think Pentium 4 hence the half-cycle latency for mov reg, reg.

See https://agner.org/optimize for numbers on newer CPUs reg-reg vs. memory mov, but note that his instruction table's load latency numbers are just part of arbitrarily dividing store/reload latency between stores and loads, and are not actually L1d-hit load-use latency.
Agner Fog's microarch guide is very good background for understanding what to do with these numbers, though.

See https://uops.info/ for good experimental test results on Intel up to about Alder Lake, and AMD up to Zen 4, which do test load-use latency (for L1d hits, like mov rax, [rax] with a pointer that points to itself). For ops like movdqa where the result can't directly be used in the next addressing-mode, they invent a chain like movdqa xmm0, [rax] / movq rax, xmm0 and assume 1c latency for other ops in the chain to get an upper bound on latency, but we know that's overly pessimistic and the real latency is a bit less.

With some clever analysis, it can be possible to figure out the exact latency of an instruction like movq rax, xmm0 and thus know the actual chain latency.

In practice yes 6 cycles is about right on most CPUs for SIMD loads, or 7 cycles for 256-bit or 512-bit loads. CPU vendors sometimes publish numbers for these in their optimization manuals, and/or in technical presentations about their newest generation of CPU design and stuff like that.

Footnote 1: I normally use https://www.felixcloutier.com/x86/, which is scraped from Intel's vol.2 PDF as of 2024-02-18 so has newer instructions, and incorporates more fixes for mistakes in older versions of the manual. The performance info on the c9x.me pages is so old it's completely irrelevant.

Q: How to flatten Entity Core many-to-many collections using Linq A:

You can flatten it by using Join() as mentioned in my comment:

return await _dbSet.AsQueryable().Join(
            dbContext.UserRoles, // DbSet of UserRole
            user => user.Id,
            userRole => userRole.UserId,
            (user, userRole) => new FlatDto
            {
                FirstName = user.FirstName,
                LastName = user.LastName,
                RoleName = userRole.Role.Name,
            }).ToListAsync();
